hints: Focus on what the two test results together tell you about the carbonyl product, aldehyde or ketone?
Remember that hydrolysis replaces each Br with OH, so check which dibromopropane puts both OH groups on the same carbon.
Apply the dehydration rule from the stem to that gem-diol and see whether you get propanal or propanone.
walkthrough:
**Decode the test results**

Think like a detective. 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine gives an orange precipitate with any carbonyl, so a positive means aldehyde or ketone.

Fehling's reagent test: $$\text{aldehyde + Fehling's} \rightarrow \text{brick-red precipitate, ketone = no reaction}$$

**Identify the target carbonyl**

Positive with 2,4-DNPH but negative with Fehling's means it cannot be an aldehyde. It must be a ketone. For $\text{C}_3$, that is propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$.

**Work backwards through hydrolysis**

Hydrolysis of a dibromoalkane replaces C-Br with C-OH:
$$\text{R-Br + OH}^- \rightarrow \text{R-OH + Br}^-$$
To get a ketone after dehydration, we need a gem-diol on carbon 2: $\text{CH}_3\text{C(OH)}_2\text{CH}_3$, which loses water:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{C(OH)}_2\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Match to the starting dibromide**

Only 2,2-dibromopropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CBr}_2\text{CH}_3$, hydrolyses to that gem-diol on carbon 2. That is why it is the precursor to the ketone.

options.A: 1,1-dibromopropane hydrolyses to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)}_2$, which dehydrates to propanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$. Propanal is an aldehyde so it is positive with both 2,4-DNPH and Fehling's, not negative with Fehling's.
options.B: 1,2-dibromopropane hydrolyses to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{OH}$, a stable 1,2-diol with OH groups on different carbons. No water is eliminated, no carbonyl forms, so it is negative with 2,4-DNPH.
options.C: 1,3-dibromopropane hydrolyses to $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, a stable 1,3-diol. Again the OH groups are on different carbons, so no carbonyl forms and the 2,4-DNPH test is negative.
options.D: 2,2-dibromopropane hydrolyses to the gem-diol $\text{CH}_3\text{C(OH)}_2\text{CH}_3$, which spontaneously loses water to give propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$. As a ketone it is positive with 2,4-DNPH but does not react with Fehling's reagent.
